paragraphs.heading: An acid coming apart
paragraphs.text: When an acid, written HA, is in solution, some of it splits into A⁻ and a hydrogen ion, H⁺. In acid–base chemistry this splitting is called dissociation, and A⁻ is called the conjugate base of the acid. The splitting and the rejoining both keep going, and once they run at the same rate the amounts stop changing; that steady state is equilibrium. For acids, chemists describe it with an equilibrium constant called the acid dissociation constant, written Kₐ.

paragraphs.heading: Ka and pKa
paragraphs.text: A lower Kₐ means a weaker acid, one that has split apart less at equilibrium. Chemists often use pKₐ instead, because it gives a convenient logarithmic scale. For a made-up weak acid with Kₐ = 10⁻⁵, log Kₐ is −5, so pKₐ = 5. Acetic acid has Kₐ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ and a pKₐ of 4.7. On this scale the direction flips: a lower pKₐ means a stronger acid.

paragraphs.heading: What sets the value
paragraphs.text: Kₐ follows directly from the thermodynamics of the dissociation, and pKₐ is directly proportional to the reaction's standard Gibbs free energy change. It also shifts with temperature, in a way Le Chatelier's principle explains. For an endothermic dissociation, warming raises Kₐ and lowers pKₐ; for an exothermic one, the reverse holds. The acid's molecular structure matters too, through inductive effects, mesomeric effects and hydrogen bonding.

paragraphs.heading: Predicting pH
paragraphs.text: You can only understand how acids and bases behave in solution, in numbers, if you know their pKₐ values. If you know the concentrations and pKₐ values of every acid and base present, you can predict the solution's pH. Going the other way, if you know the pH, you can work out how much of each acid and base is there at equilibrium. These calculations are used across chemistry, biology, medicine and geology, and pKₐ values are needed to prepare buffer solutions.

paragraphs.heading: From medicine to the ocean
paragraphs.text: Many medicines are weak acids or bases. Their pKₐ values, together with a measure called the octanol-water partition coefficient, help estimate how much of a drug gets into the bloodstream. Acidity plays a basic role in natural waters, so these constants are essential in aquatic chemistry and chemical oceanography. In living things, keeping acid–base balance and the speed of enzyme reactions both rely on the pKₐ values of all the different acids and bases found in cells and in the body.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring it
paragraphs.text: In the lab, pKₐ can be measured with a pH titration. For very low values, below about 2, or very high ones, above about 11, pH readings become hard to make in practice. In those cases spectrophotometric or NMR measurements may be needed instead.
